However, since these notes are considered anti-dilutive, including them would actually decrease (improve) the reported diluted EPS or reduce the reported loss per share in loss years. This is because the additional shares from conversion would dilute the earnings across a larger share base, but the company's net income (or loss) would remain the same.

For the years ended December 31, 2023, 2022, and 2021, NCLH explicitly excluded the exchangeable notes from diluted weighted-average shares outstanding because their inclusion would have been anti-dilutive (Chunks 1 and 2). In summary: Including the anti-dilutive exchangeable notes in the diluted EPS calculation would result in a lower diluted EPS (or a smaller loss per share), but because they are anti-dilutive, accounting standards require their exclusion.

In other words, if the exchangeable notes were hypothetically included in the calculation, the adjustment (for example, any interest benefit added back to net income) combined with the additional shares issued would result in an EPS that exceeds the basic EPS. Since the purpose of the diluted EPS measure is to show the worst‐case (lowest) EPS outcome when all dilutive instruments are considered, including instruments that increase EPS (i.e., are anti‐dilutive) is not permitted. Thus, their inclusion would artificially inflate the EPS figure relative to the basic EPS.

This point-in-time recognition means that once the performance obligation is met (i.e., the product has been delivered), the revenue is measured and recorded. 

However, in some cases--such as certain contract manufacturing agreements or other arrangements where control is transferred over time--the timing of revenue recognition may be spread out over a period. In these instances, revenue is recognized as the related performance obligations are satisfied, allowing for recognition over time rather than at a single point. Overall, the adoption of ASC 606 by Biogen refines the timing and measurement of revenue, ensuring that revenue recognition more closely mirrors the actual transfer of goods or services (either at a single point or progressively over time) based on the specific terms of each customer contract.
